https://english.radio.cz/economists-gove.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances Facebook Twitter Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances 3:36 ⨯ Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances https://english.radio.cz/economists-government-plan-loosen-fiscal-rules-threatens-public-finances-8893587#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X The opposition Civic Democrats said this week that they were prepared to take a Czech government plan to loosen rules on fiscal responsibility to the Constitutional Court. For their part, the coalition say they will overturn a presidential veto of the relevant bill in the coming weeks. Meanwhile, 20 economists have called on the government to drop the whole idea. One of them, Daniel Münich, explained the reasons for this appeal. “There are a couple of reasons. One is that it is extraordinarily important issue – simply cancelling, or more or less cancelling, important rules that limit the government and future governments in using public money. “The second reason is that it’s holiday season, and the new law seems to be moving through Parliament very easily, without major attention from people.” One thing you are against is the possibility of increasing expenditure by 10 percent on the basis of a decision by the State Security Council. But in these uncertain times, wouldn’t an extraordinary security situation justify the change the government is pushing for? “The Security Council is nothing other than part of the government, so in other words this would just be cutting out Parliament. “And it can’t be that way. The government should always go to the lower house and ask for changes in the original budget, which can be done very quickly. “So this is just a way of getting rid of Parliament.” The minister of finance, Alena Schillerová, says the government have no alternative to loosening these rules, which she calls a severe constraint on the Czech economy. “Of course that’s not true. “There is a very clear, very simple alternative. And that is to increase taxation on incomes. In 2021 there was a huge decrease that was originally planned to be temporary, but it has remained there until now. “The tax cut at that time in current prices was CZK 130 billion, which is quite a lot of money, and more than the government needs now to finance all its promises and obligations.” Some people may say that if this bill is passed and if the government then acts in an irresponsible manner, voters can punish the government – they can vote the government out or not vote for those parties again. “This government will be there until 2029, but fiscal problems, the payment of debt, will show up later on. “So the only case in which this government would be held to account by the public would be if some kind of external crisis occurred that would require much higher spending, which would impose an additional burden on the public finances.” In any case, the government are planning to override the president’s veto. The opposition say they will take the matter to the Constitutional Court. How do you think this will end? “We’ve never had such a case in this country, so it’s very difficult to say. “But my feeling is that the Constitutional Court will probably – though I’m a layman in this – say that Parliament sets the rules, so if this is approved by Parliament, by a majority in both chambers, they will have no additional say on this. “But we’ll see.” Business related articles play play Row over public spending as president vetoes government’s budget rules reform play play Helena Horská: “If you don’t feel safe, you won’t do business” play play Fitch move sparks fears of painful cut in Czech credit rating play play Can the Czech Republic “invest its way out” of the Covid-19 crisis? featured 'Great-grandmother of modern architecture': Villa Tugendhat marks 25 years on UNESCO list Why drought is unlikely to shut down Czech nuclear power plants Train or tram? https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Flowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta. Photograph: Jonathan Borg/AP View image in fullscreen Flowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta. Photograph: Jonathan Borg/AP Daphne Caruana Galizia Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial A Maltese businessman has been cleared of involvement in the journalist’s death, but his trial revealed the challenges faced by those leading the search for her killers Juliette Garside in Valletta Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.13 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers. At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia not guilty . Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes. In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government. Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two were sentenced to life in prison after pleading guilty to murder, while the third was given a reduced 15-year sentence in exchange for evidence against his accomplices. After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again. The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013. Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”. The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority. It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” View image in fullscreen Yorgen Fenech was cleared by a jury of complicity in voluntary homicide and association with the intention of committing a crime. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters While the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers. Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man. “Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury. View image in fullscreen A court artist’s sketch of Yorgen Fenech during the trial. Illustration: Anna Calleja Day The man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence. In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand. What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases. Consumed by an investigation that would kill her In the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated. As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons. View image in fullscreen Daphne Caruana Galizia in 1989 at Lisbon zoo with her sons Paul, Andrew and Matthew. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images In later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her. ‘I knew it was a car bomb straight away’: the day my mother Daphne Caruana Galizia was murdered Read more Her blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target. She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed. “I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.” Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car. It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field. View image in fullscreen Forensic experts examine the field where a bomb blew up Daphne Caruana Galizia’s rental car. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters Barricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta. “I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial. He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profit Forbidden Stories and others to form the Daphne Project . Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts. Posts she published , read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks. View image in fullscreen Caruana Galizia’s sons Matthew, Paul and Andrew and her husband, Peter, take part in a protest march in Valletta in 2019. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters Those allegations are now the subject of a criminal case, in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association. At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan. The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”. View image in fullscreen Grafitti on a wall in rural Malta highlights Caruna Galizia’s murder. Photograph: Simon Leigh/Alamy The prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations. The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been in Europe when the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested. In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma. View image in fullscreen A makeshift memorial to Caruana Galizia in Valletta, Malta. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters The mosquito and the lion For Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables. View image in fullscreen Melvin Theuma, a key witness who was granted a presidential pardon, with Judge Edwina Grima visiting the site where Caruana Galizia was killed. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters Theuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.” Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls. The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting. Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”. Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout. The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events. Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in a separate criminal case . During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found. “All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.” Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect. View image in fullscreen Malta’s former chief of staff, Keith Schembri, was a close childhood friend of Yorgen Fenech. Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty Images Under questioning, Fenech admitted paying €400,000 , via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver had “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”. He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination. “Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.” Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist. In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring. View image in fullscreen Vincent Muscat is serving a 15-year prison sentence for his part in the murder of Caruana Galizia. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters It was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name. Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.” While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled. Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.” But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planne

Photograph: Instagram/@gillymcarthur UK news ‘I could watch her for hours’: the woman who rescued a bee and created a buzz After bringing injured queen Phoebee home in July, Gilly McArthur expected her soon to die, but she’s bumbling on Amelia Hill Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Fifty-two days ago, Phoebee was lying by the side of a road in the blistering sun with a broken wing. Today, she’s clambering up the arm of Gilly McArthur, around the nape of her neck and disappearing into her hair. “I couldn’t leave her by the roadside,” McArthur says. “So I bought her home and made her a bed of flowers. I thought she’d be dead in a day or so.” Instead of dying, Phoebee did something McArthur didn’t expect: she went viral. McArthur says: “A few days after I rescued her, I was due to go on a sailing trip for a week. I couldn’t leave her here, so I took Phoebee with me – and put a post on my Instagram account of her enjoying the trip.” The following morning, McArthur woke to find messages from around the world. “It was amazing: there were so many posts from people across the globe telling me their lovely stories of capturing bumblebees or helping butterflies with broken wings – and the stories kept coming.” Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue' . Allow and continue McArthur, an author, is touched but slightly baffled by the furore. “I think it might be because the world is in such a polycrisis at the moment, and everyone is wanting to pull back to something authentic and kind,” she says. “Perhaps Phoebee reminds people of a time when bumblebees were more prolific, in a world that isn’t on fire: lots of the messages said the videos helped them feel more grounded in a world where the algorithms are usually so grounded in clickbait and violence.” Britain has 24 species of bumblebee and more than 240 species of solitary bee. Most bumblebees live for just one year. New mated queens have a bit more of a lifeline: they hibernate in the autumn and emerge in spring to establish colonies of their own. Phoebee has not mated. While McArthur does not know what that will mean for her, she is stalwart in the face of possible tragedy. “If I check on her one day and she’s not moving, I’ll check her bum. When she sleeps, her bum goes up and down very slightly,” she says. “If her bum is still, I won’t give up – I’ll put her in a quiet room and hope she’s hibernating. But her lifespan is her lifespan.” For now, McArthur spends a lot of time watching her. “She’s fascinating: she spends a lot of time cleaning herself like a cat. And I could watch her putting her long tongue out and getting the nectar out of the flowers for hours.” Andy Benson, of the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, has watched the brouhaha with similar bemusement. He thinks passions would have been cooler had Phoebee not been a buff-tailed bumblebee, the biggest and fluffiest bee, and a queen, “the biggest and fluffiest of them all”. View image in fullscreen A bumblebee on a purpletop flower in Weymouth, England in late July. Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images Benson says that while McArthur’s heroic salvation of a single bumblebee is heartwarming, the advice is to gently place lost bees on a flower and let nature take its course. “A third of British wild bees and hoverflies are in decline and a quarter of European species are at risk of extinction because of the loss of their natural habitat, climate change and bee-killing pesticides,” he says. This matters because one in three mouthfuls of our food depend on pollinators such as bees, with the crops that depend on pollination – including apples, beans, squashes and almonds – being five times more valuable than those that do not. Benson says if people want to help bees, they don’t have to take them into their home, or on a sailing trip, or let them nestle in their hair. “We can instantly help hundreds of bees in the smallest of spaces by simply planting a few flowers in their garden,” he says. McArthur knows she hasn’t stayed the plummeting bee numbers by prolonging Phoebee’s short lifespan. But she hopes she may have made a difference in another way. “Maybe this is something nice that people can pull back to and just go: ‘Oh, maybe I won’t blow my leaves away this winter – maybe I might plant more plants for pollinators – maybe I might just stop and look at the smaller things with more curiosity’,” she says. “And maybe Phoebee’s videos will help people realise that looking at the smaller things in more detail can make the bigger things feel more manageable.” Explore more on these topics UK news Bees Insects Wildlife Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/09/mask.text: A federal immigration officer shot and wounded a Dominican man while arresting him in New York City on Thursday, during what the Department of Homeland Security called a “targeted enforcement operation.”Protesters and local officials decried it as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.The man survived and is being treated at a hospital, the agency said. It did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that “during the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon” and that the man was injured.New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Governor Kathy Hochul said they had received reports the agents fired at the man while he was inside a vehicle with a 5-year-old child, who was apparently unhurt.Hochul said she had urged US President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin by phone to halt immigration enforcement actions in New York.Mamdani said in a statement he also wanted ICE actions to stop in the city, calling the shooting “unconscionable and incredibly serious.”The gunfire erupted around 4 pm local time in Marble Hill, a small part of Manhattan that is attached to the Bronx borough.Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming.Bystander videos and photos posted on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle.Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. The videos show agents wearing ICE badges on the scene, including one carrying a rifle.Protesters at the scene chanted, “ICE off our streets now!” and then marched to the hospital where the injured man was being treated.A sizable crowd blocked an intersection at the hospital entry, and as police began to set barricades so that ambulances and other vehicles could pass, some protesters shoved past the barriers and hurled water bottles at officers.DHS complained that its officers “are forced to make arrests at large in the community in unpredictable and dangerous environments” when “dangerous illegal aliens" get released.The agency blamed “reckless sanctuary policies” in Democrat-led areas. There is no clear definition of sanctuary jurisdictions, but the term is generally applied to state and local governments that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.The agency said the man who was shot had a prior grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. New York police arrested him in December 2023, and he was released, DHS added.ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen vehicle stops since last year, killing at least four people and wounding others.In late September, ICE ordered its officers not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck0e.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, El Salvadoran military vehicles arrive in the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince By Harry Sekulich Published 5 hours ago El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago. The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday. Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued. Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti. The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility. The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations". Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match. He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform. Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans. In October last year , the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti. The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital. Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel MoÃ¯se in 2021.
